term: "K-Fold Cross-Validation"
letter: "K"

## Simple explanation

K-fold cross-validation checks how well a model generalizes by repeatedly
training on most of the data and validating on a different held-out subset.
This helps reduce the risk that one lucky split creates a misleading result.

## Technical explanation

The dataset is divided into $K$ roughly equal subsets, or folds. For each
iteration, one fold is reserved for validation and the remaining $K-1$ folds
are used for training. The model is trained and evaluated $K$ times, and the
final score is often the mean or median of the validation scores. This yields
an estimate of average expected performance under data variation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Cross-validation is a standard way to estimate model quality and tune
hyperparameters without using the final evaluation data too early. It is
particularly useful when the dataset is limited and small fluctuations in the
holdout split could otherwise distort conclusions.

## How it works

1. Shuffle and split the data into $K$ folds.
2. Train on $K-1$ folds.
3. Validate on the held-out fold.
4. Repeat until each fold has served as validation once.
5. Aggregate the validation scores.

If the fold sizes are balanced and the data distribution is representative,
this yields a stronger estimate than a single train/test split.

## Practical example

Suppose a team has 1,000 labeled customer-support tickets and wants to test a
text classifier. They use 5-fold cross-validation, training on 4 folds and
validating on the 5th, then repeat the process 5 times. The average F1 score
helps estimate real-world performance more reliably than one single split.

## Common misconceptions

- Cross-validation does not replace a final holdout test set for the final
  model claim.
- A random split is not always enough: time-based or group-based splits may
  be required for some tasks.
- More folds can reduce variance but increase computational cost.
